stories.title: Fix PowerShell command injection in the Windows keychain provider
stories.user_story: As a Windows user, I want `${keychain:...}` references resolved without letting a config value execute arbitrary PowerShell, so a tampered or synced config can't run code on my machine.
stories.context: Review finding (BLOCKER, verified). packages/secrets/src/providers/keychain.ts:32-40 interpolates the untrusted `account` (the path in `${keychain:path}`, which core's SECRET_REF_RE at schema.ts:68 allows as `.+`) directly into a single-quoted PowerShell -Command string: `(Get-StoredCredential -Target '${service}:${account}').GetNetworkCredential().Password`. A ref such as `${keychain:x'); Start-Process calc; ('}` closes the quote and executes injected statements. Secrets resolve at run/test time (commands/run.ts), and env-channel refs are not covered by the TOFU gate, so this is reachable for a tampered config even on an otherwise-trusted server. The POSIX branches pass `account` as an argv element (no shell); only the Windows branch string-interpolates.
acceptance_criteria: The Windows keychain provider never interpolates account/service into a -Command script string; the value is passed out-of-band (a bound argv parameter via `-- <account>`, an env var, or -EncodedCommand).
A ${keychain:...} account containing a single quote, semicolon, ), $( , backtick, or newline resolves as a literal lookup key and cannot execute a command.
Behavior parity: a normal keychain account still resolves on win32.
Defense in depth: tighten core SECRET_REF_RE so the path excludes shell/quote metacharacters (coordinate with S22.22).
tests: Unit: an injection-payload account does not alter the executed argv beyond the parameterized value, and no extra command runs.
Unit: a normal account still resolves on win32.
definition_of_done: Windows keychain resolution is injection-proof, proven by a test that feeds a metacharacter-laden account and asserts no command execution.

stories.title: Merge into shared-state client files instead of overwriting them
stories.user_story: As a user of Claude Code, Zed, Gemini CLI, or VS Code, I want `mcpfold sync` to update only the MCP-servers section of my client config and preserve everything else, so folding my servers never wipes my login, editor settings, or history.
stories.context: Review finding (BLOCKER, data loss, verified). The sync engine reads the on-disk file and passes it as `existing` to adapter.render (commands/sync.ts:138-143; MCPAdapter.render accepts existing?, types.ts:104). Merge-aware adapters (codex-cli/goose/opencode) consume it, but the shared factory createMcpServersAdapter.render (packages/adapters/src/shared.ts:249-261), gemini-cli's custom render (gemini-cli.ts:70), and vscode (vscode.ts:105) omit the existing parameter and emit serialize({ [rootKey]: shape }) - a full replacement. claude-code user scope resolves to ~/.claude.json (Claude Code's entire user state: OAuth account, project history, numStartups), zed to ~/.config/zed/settings.json and .zed/settings.json (all editor settings), gemini-cli to ~/.gemini/settings.json (auth type, theme). The first sync destroys all non-MCP content. claude_desktop_config.json can also hold non-MCP keys (e.g. globalShortcut).
acceptance_criteria: The shared full-replace factory (and any adapter whose target is not a dedicated MCP file) merges: parse existing, replace only the MCP-servers root key, and preserve every other top-level key.
claude-code (user), zed (user + project), gemini-cli (user + project), and vscode preserve all non-MCP keys on write.
claude-desktop is audited; if its target file can hold non-MCP keys, it merges too.
Dedicated files (.mcp.json project scope, canonical mcp.config.jsonc) may remain full-replace.
Merge preserves formatting/comments for JSONC client files (jsonc-parser modify/applyEdits, as opencode does).
tests: Per-adapter: render with an existing file containing unrelated top-level keys preserves them; only the servers key changes.
Round-trip: seed a realistic ~/.claude.json / zed settings.json with extra keys and assert they survive a sync write.
definition_of_done: Syncing to claude-code/zed/gemini-cli/vscode never drops non-MCP content, proven by round-trip tests seeded with real-world extra keys.

stories.title: Reject __proto__/constructor keys in the core config parser
stories.user_story: As a user, I want a malformed or hostile config to fail validation rather than silently validate as empty, so the strict schema can't be bypassed and my real servers can't vanish.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH, schema bypass, verified at runtime). packages/core/src/load.ts:180-187 nodeToValue reconstructs objects with obj[key] = nodeToValue(...). Bracket assignment to __proto__ invokes the prototype setter, so a `__proto__` property mutates the object's prototype instead of creating an own property. Confirmed: loadConfig of a document whose whole body is nested under __proto__ returns ok:true with zero own keys - the .strict() schema is fully bypassed and any real servers/profiles nested there silently disappear. detectVersion reads version through the prototype chain, so prototype content also drives version detection. A server literally named __proto__ corrupts the servers record.
acceptance_criteria: nodeToValue builds objects with Object.create(null) or explicitly skips/rejects the keys __proto__, constructor, and prototype, emitting a positioned schema error for a literal __proto__ key.
The same hardening is applied in serialize.ts sortKeysDeep and the migration spreads.
A config whose body is nested under __proto__ returns ok:false (schema error), not a silently-empty valid config.
Real content under a normal key is never dropped.
tests: Unit: __proto__-bodied and __proto__-named-server payloads return ok:false; a normal config is unaffected.
definition_of_done: The untrusted parse path cannot be bypassed via __proto__/constructor, proven by tests.

stories.title: Include env in the TOFU executable signature (NODE_OPTIONS/LD_PRELOAD)
stories.user_story: As a user with trusted MCP servers, I want a change to a server's environment to force re-approval, so a tampered config can't inject code via env vars behind my back.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH, verified). packages/cli/src/trust/tofu.ts:31-38 executableSignature hashes only command, args, and pin. run.ts:235 spawns the child with { ...process.env, ...(s.env ?? {}) }. Server env is a first-class code-execution channel: NODE_OPTIONS=--require /evil.js (any node/npx server), LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, DYLD_*, PYTHONSTARTUP, PYTHONPATH, BROWSER. Because env is outside the signed surface, a synced config can change a trusted server's env and it runs with no CHANGED / re-approve gate; pull.ts:169 even auto-approves via gate.approve.
acceptance_criteria: executableSignature includes a canonicalized (sorted keys+values) form of env, or at minimum pins a denylist of code-execution env vars (NODE_OPTIONS, LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, DYLD_*, PYTHONSTARTUP, PYTHONPATH, BROWSER) so any change forces re-approval.
Adding NODE_OPTIONS to a previously-trusted server flips the trust decision to changed / needs-approval.
run does not spawn the child until the changed server is re-approved.
tests: Unit: mutating a trusted server's env changes the signature / trust decision.
definition_of_done: A trusted server whose env is altered by a pulled config is re-gated before it can run.

stories.title: Back up the canonical config before pull --yes overwrites it
stories.user_story: As a user, I want `mcpfold pull` to back up my local canonical config before applying a remote version, so I can recover uncommitted local edits if I pull the wrong thing.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH, data loss, verified). commands/pull.ts:165 calls atomicWrite(target, serialize(remote.config)) with no prior backupIfExists (pull.ts imports only atomicWrite). Every other canonical-config writer backs up first: migrate.ts:80 and sync.ts:173 both call backupIfExists before atomicWrite. restore only enumerates client files via adapter.resolvePath per profile (restore.ts:47-56) and never targets the canonical mcp.config.jsonc, so a clobbered canonical config with uncommitted edits is unrecoverable.
acceptance_criteria: runPull calls backupIfExists(target) immediately before atomicWrite.
The backup path is returned in PullData and surfaced in the human output (mirroring migrate/sync).
Optionally, restore learns to enumerate the canonical file so a pulled overwrite can be undone.
tests: Integration: a pre-existing canonical config is backed up before a pull applies; the backup path appears in output.
definition_of_done: pull --yes never overwrites the canonical config without leaving a timestamped backup.

stories.title: Enforce recursion-depth limits in core traversals (parse/serialize/diff)
stories.user_story: As a user, I want a pathologically nested config to be rejected cleanly rather than crash the tool, so a typo or hostile file can't DoS mcpfold.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH, DoS, verified at runtime). packages/core/src/load.ts:177-194 nodeToValue, serialize.ts:23-34 sortKeysDeep, and diff's semanticEqual recurse once per nesting level with no depth cap. Confirmed: a config with ~200k nested brackets makes loadConfig throw an uncaught RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, violating the documented no-throw LoadResult contract.
acceptance_criteria: A maximum nesting depth (e.g. 64) is enforced during parse and traversal; exceeding it returns a positioned schema/parse error (ok:false), never throws.
sortKeysDeep and semanticEqual are depth-capped or iterative.
A config with pathological nesting returns ok:false cleanly.
tests: Unit: deeply nested input returns a positioned error instead of throwing.
definition_of_done: No config text can make core throw a RangeError; deep nesting is a clean validation error.

stories.title: Keep loadConfig's no-throw contract for malformed version numbers
stories.user_story: As a user, I want a config with a bad version number to produce a clear error rather than crash doctor/sync, so one typo doesn't take down the tool.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH, verified at runtime). load.ts:132-135 calls migrateConfig(value, SCHEMA_VERSION) with no try/catch whenever detectVersion(value) < 2. detectVersion (migrate/index.ts:17-26) accepts any number verbatim - 0, negatives, fractionals. migrateConfig then loops while (current < target) and throws MigrationError when no step has from === current. Confirmed: version 0 and version 1.5 both throw uncaught, crashing any consumer that relies on the documented no-throw LoadResult (doctor, sync).
acceptance_criteria: loadConfig converts a thrown MigrationError into an ok:false PositionedError (code schema).
detectVersion rejects non-integer or < 1 versions as a schema error before migrating.
Configs with version 0, -1, and 1.5 all return ok:false rather than throwing.
tests: Unit: version 0 / -1 / 1.5 each yield ok:false.
definition_of_done: Malformed version numbers never throw out of loadConfig.

stories.title: Parse client configs tolerantly (JSONC) and never crash on malformed input
stories.user_story: As a user, I want `mcpfold import` and drift detection to handle a client config that has comments or a small mistake, so a valid JSONC file or a corrupt file gives a clear error instead of a raw crash.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH, verified). Every adapter parse() uses JSON.parse with no try/catch (shared.ts:263, vscode.ts:125, gemini-cli.ts:83, opencode.ts:100, and others). VS Code mcp.json, Cursor mcp.json, Claude Code config, and Roo/Cline settings are officially JSONC (comments and trailing commas are allowed and common). JSON.parse throws an uncaught SyntaxError on those, and on any user-corrupted file. opencode's own render can even emit JSONC its parse then can't read.
acceptance_criteria: JSONC clients are parsed with a tolerant parser (jsonc-parser, already a dependency).
Every adapter parse is wrapped so a malformed or commented file raises a UsageError naming the file, never a raw exception.
import and drift detection handle a commented client file and a corrupt file gracefully.
tests: Unit: a JSONC file with comments parses cleanly; a corrupt file yields a UsageError, not a SyntaxError.
definition_of_done: No third-party client config can crash import/drift with a raw parser exception.

stories.title: Wire package-integrity (SRI) verification end-to-end
stories.user_story: As a user who pins an integrity hash on a stdio server, I want the fetched package's bytes actually verified against it, so the supply-chain control is real and not decorative.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM, combined + verified). packages/cli/src/trust/integrity.ts exports verifyPackageIntegrity and computeIntegrity, but a grep shows they are never called anywhere - only parseIntegrity is used, and only to warn on malformed syntax (checks/servers.ts:56). The supply-chain control is dead. Separately, core resolve.ts:42-60 toResolved never copies server.integrity onto ResolvedServer (types.ts has no integrity field), so the hash can't reach the fetch/install layer even once verification is wired.
acceptance_criteria: integrity propagates through resolution: ResolvedServer gains integrity? and toResolved sets integrity: server.integrity.
The fetch/install/pin path computes the fetched tarball hash and calls verifyPackageIntegrity, failing closed on a mismatch with a clear supply-chain error.
A declared-but-mismatching integrity blocks the operation.
Tests cover propagation and match/mismatch/malformed.
tests: Unit: integrity survives resolution; a mismatching hash fails closed.
definition_of_done: A pinned integrity hash is enforced against fetched bytes, proven by a mismatch test.

stories.title: Cap the proxy stdio read buffer and handle stream errors/close
stories.user_story: As a user running the curation proxy, I want a malicious or crashing MCP server to be contained, so it can't OOM the proxy or take it down with an uncaught stream error.
stories.context: Review finding (HIGH + MEDIUM, verified). packages/proxy/src/transport/stdio.ts:14-24 onData does buffer += chunk and only drains up to the last newline, with no maximum. A server (the untrusted party the proxy exists to contain) can stream megabytes/gigabytes with no newline and the proxy accumulates it all. The transport also registers only input.on('data', ...) - no 'error'/'end'/'close' handler - so a stream error (EPIPE when the child dies) becomes an uncaught exception; close() only removes the data listener and never destroys the stream, and residual bytes after the final newline are dropped silently on EOF.
acceptance_criteria: A maximum buffered-line length (a few MB, configurable) is enforced; exceeding it closes the connection with an error instead of growing.
input 'error'/'end'/'close' are handled and surfaced as a clean shutdown.
close() removes all listeners and destroys the stream.
A test streams an over-cap line and asserts bounded memory plus a clean error.
tests: Unit: over-cap unterminated input closes with an error; a stream error does not crash the proxy.
definition_of_done: The proxy survives a server that floods stdout or crashes mid-write.

stories.title: Validate registry-supplied runtime hints and remote URLs before writing configs
stories.user_story: As a user, I want the launch command mcpfold writes into my client configs to come from a known-safe set, so a malicious registry mirror can't make me run an arbitrary command.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM, security, verified). packages/cli/src/registry/map.ts:50-64 runnerFor returns pkg.runtimeHint ?? 'npx'. runtimeHint is server-controlled data from server.json and flows directly into server.command (the process the client will spawn), with only the pinned package spec as args. A registry entry can set runtimeHint to an arbitrary command string. remote.url (map.ts:124) is also written into client configs without validating it is https.
acceptance_criteria: Runners are whitelisted: known registryType/runtimeHint values map to npx/uvx/docker/etc.; an unknown runtime hint is rejected with a UsageError, never passed through as the command.
remote.url must be an https URL before it is written into a client config.
Tests cover a hostile runtimeHint and a non-https url.
tests: Unit: an arbitrary runtimeHint is rejected; a non-https remote url is rejected.
definition_of_done: Registry data can only produce a whitelisted runner and an https remote url.

stories.title: Close proxy tool-filter bypasses (notification-form call, alias/case)
stories.user_story: As a user relying on the curation proxy's deny list, I want a blocked tool to stay blocked no matter how the call is shaped, so the filter is a real boundary.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM, security, verified). packages/proxy/src/proxy.ts:112 gates the tools/call rejection on message.id !== undefined, so a tools/call sent as a notification (no id) skips the !isToolAllowed check and is forwarded to the server at proxy.ts:134 - a blocked tool executes fire-and-forget. Separately, filter.ts:14-22 isToolAllowed uses exact directive.list.includes(name), so a deny-listed tool the server also honors under a different case/whitespace/namespace spelling (FOO, 'foo ', pkg:foo) passes the filter.
acceptance_criteria: The tool filter is applied to tools/call regardless of id presence; a notification-form call to a filtered tool is dropped or rejected, never forwarded.
Tool-name matching is normalized consistently on both the tools/list filter and the tools/call guard (or non-canonical forms are rejected).
Tests cover a notification-form blocked call and a case/namespace-variant name.
tests: Unit: a notification-form blocked call is not forwarded; a case-variant name is treated per the deny policy.
definition_of_done: A filtered tool cannot reach the server via a notification or a spelling variant.

stories.title: Bound proxy pending maps and validate the handshake protocol version
stories.user_story: As a user, I want the proxy to stay bounded and speak only a protocol version it understands, so a slow or hostile server can't leak memory or push an unsupported version.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM x2, verified). packages/proxy/src/proxy.ts pendingToolListing (proxy.ts:132) and audit inflight (audit.ts:93) only shrink on a matching response; a server that never replies (or replies with an error/non-tools result) leaks an entry per request, with no TTL or size cap. handshake.ts:154-160 accepts init.protocolVersion unconditionally (protocolSupported is computed at line 166 but never gates anything), sends notifications/initialized and tools/list regardless, and then echoes the attacker-chosen version string as the MCP-Protocol-Version header on every later request (mcp-transport.ts:51-53); init may also be null.
acceptance_criteria: A tracked id is evicted on ANY response for that id (forward unfiltered if it isn't a tools result).
The audit inflight map has a TTL or size cap so stale ids are dropped.
The handshake validates init is a non-null object and, when the negotiated version is unsupported, does not send initialized/tools/list (returns protocolSupported:false or fails per policy).
Tests cover a leaking id and an unsupported version.
tests: Unit: unmatched ids don't accumulate; an unsupported protocol version aborts the handshake.
definition_of_done: The proxy's pending state is bounded and it refuses unsupported protocol versions.

stories.title: Pass the macOS session secret over stdin, not argv
stories.user_story: As a macOS user, I want my session tokens kept out of the process argument list, so another local process can't read them from ps while login runs.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM, verified). packages/cli/src/cloud/token-store.ts:68-71 - the darwin set command is `security add-generic-password -U -s mcpfold -a <account> -w <secret>`, placing the serialized CloudSession (both access and refresh tokens) directly in argv. The module docstring and the Linux (line 83) and Windows (line 124) branches deliberately use stdin (never argv); only the macOS branch inlines the value.
acceptance_criteria: The darwin set command uses -w with no inline value and feeds the secret over stdin, matching the Linux/Windows branches.
run() writes stdin for the set command.
The secret never appears in argv on any platform.
A test asserts the darwin set command carries the secret via stdin, not args.
tests: Unit: darwin set specifies stdin and omits the secret from args.
definition_of_done: No mcpfold-spawned credential command exposes a secret in argv.

stories.title: Validate the cloud refresh response before persisting the session
stories.user_story: As a user, I want a malformed token-refresh response to surface an error rather than silently log me out, so my session state stays consistent.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM, verified). packages/cli/src/cloud/api.ts:113-117 refresh returns (await res.json()) as RefreshResponse with no shape check - unlike pollDevice, which validates tokens at the source (S16.6, lines 96-104). session.ts:41-49 then trusts it: accessToken: refreshed.access_token and expiresAt: now + refreshed.expires_in. A 200 response missing access_token/expires_in yields accessToken undefined (JSON.stringify drops it, so loadSession later returns null and silently logs the user out) and expiresAt NaN (defeats the still-valid check, so every call re-refreshes).
acceptance_criteria: refresh validates access_token is a non-empty string and expires_in is finite before returning and/or before saveSession, reusing the pollDevice validation.
A malformed 200 surfaces a clear error instead of corrupting the stored session.
A test covers a missing-field 200.
tests: Unit: a refresh 200 missing access_token/expires_in does not persist a corrupt session.
definition_of_done: A bad refresh response can't silently log the user out or spin re-refreshes.

stories.title: Back up and atomically write on import --force, and re-validate the merged config
stories.user_story: As a user, I want `mcpfold import --force` to back up my existing config, write atomically, and refuse to persist an invalid result, so an import can't corrupt or silently break my canonical config.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM + LOW, verified). commands/import.ts:246 uses writeFileSync(configPath, contents) - the --force overwrite path (the no-force case is guarded at line 159) takes no backupIfExists and is not atomic, unlike migrate/sync/add. import also writes without a loadConfig round-trip (add.ts:231-236 and init.ts:72-75 validate; import doesn't), so a client file that parses into a shape the canonical schema rejects yields an invalid mcp.config.jsonc on disk.
acceptance_criteria: import routes the write through atomicWrite and calls backupIfExists when the file already exists.
import runs loadConfig on the merged result and raises a ConfigValidationError (or warns listing the offending servers) instead of persisting an invalid canonical file.
Tests cover force-overwrite backup and an invalid merge.
tests: Integration: import --force backs up first; an invalid merge is rejected, not written.
definition_of_done: import --force is atomic, backed up, and never writes an invalid canonical config.

stories.title: Make watchWithDebounce swallow onChange rejections (honor never-throws contract)
stories.user_story: As a user running `mcpfold sync --watch`, I want a transient error in a change handler to be contained, so the watch keeps running instead of crashing the process.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM, verified). packages/cli/src/io/watch.ts:74 invokes the async fire as void fire() (and re-invokes via schedule() in the finally re-run path). If onChange returns a rejected promise, fire's promise rejects and, discarded with void, becomes an unhandled promise rejection - process-terminating on modern Node. The module's own doc (lines 37-38) promises the primitive never throws or dies. runSyncWatch happens to wrap its work in try/catch, but watchWithDebounce is a public export (index.ts:43) and the contract is unmet for any other caller.
acceptance_criteria: fire catches internally so an onChange rejection can never escape (or every call site uses .catch).
A test with a rejecting onChange produces no unhandled rejection and the watch keeps running.
tests: Unit: a rejecting onChange does not surface an unhandled rejection.
definition_of_done: watchWithDebounce honors its documented never-throws contract.

stories.title: Add a request timeout and response/zip size limits to the registry client
stories.user_story: As a user, I want registry calls to fail fast and bounded, so a slow or malicious mirror can't hang the CLI or exhaust memory.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM + LOW, verified). packages/cli/src/registry/client.ts:49 fetchImpl(url, { headers }) sets no AbortSignal/timeout, so a mirror that accepts the connection but never responds hangs the CLI forever (contradicting the S0.9 fail-clearly contract). client.ts:64 res.json() reads an unbounded body, and registry/mcpb.ts:54-56 unzipSync decompresses a .mcpb bundle with no size or entry-count cap (fflate has no zip-bomb guard).
acceptance_criteria: Registry fetches attach AbortSignal.timeout and surface a timeout via the existing degraded-mode UsageError.
A maximum content length is enforced on registry responses.
A maximum decompressed size / entry count is enforced when reading manifest.json, aborting past the threshold.
Tests cover a timeout and an oversize response/bundle.
tests: Unit: a non-responding mirror times out; an oversized bundle is rejected.
definition_of_done: Registry access is time-bounded and size-bounded.

stories.title: Fix policy package matching (segment boundary) and glob ReDoS
stories.user_story: As an org admin, I want allow/deny policy rules to match exactly the packages I name and evaluate in linear time, so governance isn't silently over/under-applied or hung by a glob.
stories.context: Review finding (MEDIUM + LOW, verified). packages/core/src/policy.ts:114-118 - the package matcher is stripVersion(pkg).startsWith(rule.package) || pkg.startsWith(rule.package), a raw startsWith with no path/segment boundary, so a rule for @modelcontextprotocol/server-git matches @modelcontextprotocol/server-github, and foo matches foo-bar (over/under-matching for a deny-wins control). policy.ts:101-104 globToRe maps each * to .* with no collapsing, so a url glob with ** compiles to adjacent .* groups - catastrophic backtracking against a long server.url.
acceptance_criteria: The package matcher requires a name boundary: exact versionless-spec equality, or the next character after the prefix is /, @, or end-of-string.
Runs of * collapse to a single .* (or a linear segment matcher replaces the regex) before compiling.
Tests cover a sibling-package non-match and a ** glob against a long non-matching url with bounded time.
tests: Unit: server-git rule does not match server-github; a ** url glob evaluates in bounded time.
definition_of_done: Policy matching is boundary-correct and ReDoS-free.

stories.title: Harden atomicWrite (durability + symlink) and use it in export/init
stories.user_story: As a user, I want config writes to be crash-durable and to not silently replace my symlinked config files, and I want every config writer to be atomic.
stories.context: Review finding (LOW, verified). packages/cli/src/io/atomic-write.ts:26 gives atomic content replacement but no fsync of the file or directory, so the documented crash-mid-write-leaves-original-intact guarantee is weaker than stated (a power-loss just after renameSync can lose the rename or leave a zero-length file). renameSync over a symlinked target replaces the link with a regular file (backupIfExists's copyFileSync reads through the link), silently destroying a user's symlinked config on the next sync. Separately, export.ts:167 and init.ts:90 use bare writeFileSync (a torn read is possible when export --force overwrites a file another tool is reading).
acceptance_criteria: Optionally fsync the temp fd before rename and the directory after, if the durability claim is to hold.
Symlink intent is decided and documented (resolve realpathSync if links should be followed).
export and init write via atomicWrite.
tests: Unit: export/init use atomicWrite; symlink behavior matches the documented intent.
definition_of_done: All config writers are atomic and atomicWrite's durability/symlink behavior matches its docs.

stories.title: Validate numeric CLI flags and harden dotenv secret set
stories.user_story: As a user, I want bad numeric flags to be rejected and `mcpfold secret set` to write .env safely, so flags don't silently misbehave and secrets don't leak or duplicate.
stories.context: Review finding (LOW x2, verified). cli.ts:530 and :639 coerce --limit and --config-version with Number() and never reject NaN/negative/non-integer, forwarding garbage to the registry/cloud client (--limit abc becomes NaN; --config-version 1.5 stays non-integer). commands/secret.ts:84 appendFileSync(envPath, `${parsed.path}=${options.value}\n`, { mode: 0o600 }) appends unconditionally: parsed.path ([^}]+) and value are unescaped (a newline injects extra KEY=VALUE lines), duplicate keys accumulate (last-wins masks stale values), and mode 0o600 only applies when .env is created - a pre-existing 0644 .env stays world-readable.
acceptance_criteria: --limit and --config-version parse via a validated integer helper that throws UsageError on NaN/negative (and non-integer for version).
dotenv secret set rejects path/value containing newline or =, upserts an existing key instead of blind-appending, and chmods 0600 after writing on POSIX.
Tests cover bad flags and an injection value.
tests: Unit: --limit abc and --config-version 1.5 raise UsageError; a newline in a secret value is rejected.
definition_of_done: Numeric flags are validated and dotenv writes are safe and idempotent.

stories.title: Tighten redaction prefixes and unify the secret-ref grammar
stories.user_story: As a user, I want all common token formats reliably redacted and secret references parsed consistently, so a secret can't slip into logs and doctor/resolver agree on a ref's path.
stories.context: Review finding (LOW x2, verified). packages/cli/src/util/redact.ts:29-34 KNOWN_TOKEN_RE omits GitHub fine-grained PATs (github_pat_) and Stripe secret keys (sk_live_/sk_test_; note sk- requires a hyphen, Stripe uses _), leaving them to the fragile HIGH_ENTROPY_RE heuristic; refguard.ts RAW_SECRET already covers github_pat_, so the two lists are inconsistent. packages/core/src/secret-ref.ts:29-32 WHOLE_REF_RE uses greedy (.+) while EMBEDDED_REF_RE uses ([^}]+), so ${env:a}b} parses to path a}b vs a between the whole and embedded paths; SECRET_REF_RE (schema.ts:68) also uses .+.
acceptance_criteria: KNOWN_TOKEN_RE adds github_pat_ and sk_(live|test)_ and is aligned with refguard's RAW_SECRET list.
Whole-ref and embedded-ref parsing use the same non-} path class and agree on ${env:a}b}.
SECRET_REF_RE is updated consistently (coordinate with S22.1's grammar tightening).
Tests cover the new prefixes and the ambiguous ref.
tests: Unit: github_pat_ and sk_live_ are masked by the known-prefix rule; whole/embedded parsing agree.
definition_of_done: All common token prefixes redact and the secret-ref grammar is single-sourced.

stories.title: Fix adapter/migration round-trip fidelity and residual __proto__ handling
stories.user_story: As a user, I want import/export round-trips to preserve transports and my configs, and hostile keys to be neutralized everywhere they're rebuilt, so fidelity and pinning integrity hold.
stories.context: Review finding (LOW, several, verified). packages/adapters/src/shared.ts:122-125,191-194 - for url-shape clients (Cursor/Zed/Cline/Warp/LM Studio) an sse remote is written as a bare url with no transport marker, so fromMcpServersShape re-reads it as streamable-http (transport lost on export->import). migrate/migrations.ts:25-33 synthesizes servers:{} when a v1 file omits servers, masking the required-field error. Adapter servers maps are built with plain-object assignment (shared.ts:174-203 and vscode/gemini/opencode/codex/goose) and proxy tool-digest.ts:31-33 sortDeep assigns __proto__ via computed key, so a server named __proto__ or a schema __proto__ key is mishandled or evades the pinning schemaDigest (S18.1 drift).
acceptance_criteria: SSE transport is preserved for url-shape clients where possible, or the coercion is documented.
The v1->v2 migration preserves the absence of servers so the required-field error still fires.
Adapter servers maps and proxy sortDeep use Object.create(null) or skip __proto__/constructor so hostile keys can't corrupt the map or evade schemaDigest.
Tests cover an SSE round-trip and a __proto__-named server.
tests: Unit: an sse remote survives export->import; a __proto__ key is neutralized in adapters and the digest.
definition_of_done: Round-trips preserve transports and hostile keys can't corrupt maps or the pinning digest.

stories.title: Reduce proxy audit-sink syscalls and use a Set for the tool directive
stories.user_story: As a user with auditing on, I want the audit sink to be cheap and reliable and tool filtering to be O(1), so per-call overhead and lost audit records are avoided.
stories.context: Review finding (LOW x2, verified). packages/proxy/src/audit.ts:139-147 fileAuditSink does mkdirSync(recursive) + statSync + appendFileSync (three syscalls) per event, and its size-check then renameSync rotation is a check-then-act with no locking, so concurrent proxies sharing a log path can both stat-under-limit then both rename/append, losing or clobbering records. filter.ts:14-22 isToolAllowed does directive.list.includes(name) - an O(n) scan per tool giving O(n*m) filtering, on the tools/call hot path.
acceptance_criteria: The audit directory is created once (cached), a running byte counter avoids per-write statSync, and rotation is atomic or uses per-process filenames.
The directive is precomputed into a Set for O(1) membership on both filtering and the call guard.
Tests/bench as feasible.
tests: Unit: directive membership is Set-based; audit rotation doesn't lose records under concurrent writers.
definition_of_done: Auditing is low-overhead and race-safe, and tool filtering is O(1) per tool.
